But the investors financing this engine of the artificial-intelligence revolution aren’t paying enough attention to the terms of their lending. Some of the deals being underwritten offer proper protections against construction delays or problem tenants; others, much less so. Bondholders need to get a grip on the detail in the documents before things start to go awry.
The five hyperscalers – Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Oracle Corp. – are
expected to invest $5.8 trillion in the computing capacity they need to run AI by 2030

, according to estimates from Goldman Sachs Group Inc. All apart from Oracle have very healthy cash flows, but that income and more will be ploughed into chips, servers and the vast sheds in which they’re housed.

The big five have already raised billions of dollars from corporate bond sales in the past 18 months, including nearly $200 billion just this year. At the same time, several have used off-balance-sheet joint ventures to fund individual data centers with about $90 billion raised against more than a dozen projects.

These standalone JV deals will remain an important source of money for the AI buildout, because the industry’s funding needs are so vast it will have to tap as many kinds of debt as it can. Despite the complexity and variety of terms in these deals, bond buyers have focused more on the attractions of backing the big tech companies and the AI trend rather than scrutinizing the details of each project.

Take the nearly $11 billion of bonds tied to three data centers for cloud-operating startup FluidStack Ltd., backstopped by Alphabet’s Google division. Each project has raised dedicated funding via privately placed bonds for structures that will be leased by FluidStack when completed. The underwriting shortcut is to rely on the strength of Alphabet as guarantor — but some of the terms are very different. One has a full guarantee from Google to assume the lease if the cloud operator fails, which is great for the lenders. Another has a guarantee from Google but at a 25% rental discount, according to analysts at Citigroup Inc. The third has a formula for the rent that Google would pay linked to operating costs. The backstops for the latter two should cover the debt costs, but they offer less comfort than the first. There are further differences. One of these deals has a guaranteed maximum price of construction agreed with the engineers building it, a clause that’s missing from the other two, which might be less good for the health of the project. Another variation: One project has a clause that lets FluidStack and Google walk away if construction is delayed by more than six months, which would be terrible for bondholders. There are more examples of friendly and unfriendly lender terms in these deals and others that are critical to judging the risks of a default. Only one of the FluidStack deals got an investment grade credit score from ratings companies — the $3.25 billion HUT 8 DC LLC project in St Francisville, Louisiana, which has a full lease guarantee from Google, a maximum construction price and no walk-away rights for the tenant.

But the borrowing costs of most data center JVs are similar despite the wide variety of terms, and the bond values move closely in line with each other, suggesting little investor discrimination between them. Investors have treated the asset class as homogenous, according to credit analysts at Goldman Sachs. They suspect yields will diverge more over time as the protections — or lack thereof — become more important.

which could be good for future lenders. But it also means deals are likely to remain idiosyncratic, rather than the market converging on standard terms. Everyone needs to keep studying the documentation closely. Given this complexity, why don’t Google and its peers just issue cheaper, simpler corporate bonds to fund this massive infrastructure bet? Apart from Oracle, most have very little debt on their books and could afford to borrow hundreds of billions each in this way.
